The Laysan albatross (Phoebastria immutabilis) begins its life cycle within a calcareous egg incubated at a mean nest temperature of 36 °C [T = 36 °C], a thermal regime that facilitates embryonic development over a period of approximately 64 days [ab = approximately 64 days]. The freshly laid egg weighs approximately 288 grams [Ww0 = approximately 288 grams], a substantial initial investment in a single offspring. Upon hatching, the newly emerged altricial nestling weighs roughly 167 grams [Wwb = roughly 167 grams], a relatively modest mass that reflects the substantial yolk reserves that have been metabolized during the latter stages of incubation. This initial wet weight is quickly supplanted by rapid mass gain as both parents begin intensive provisioning. The development of the downy chick is heavily dependent on the regular delivery of regurgitated prey, primarily squid and fish, which fuels a period of accelerated growth. During these early weeks, the nestling remains brooded almost continuously, relying on the thermal environment provided by the attending adults until it can effectively thermoregulate on its own.

As the nestling matures, it enters a phase of rapid mass increase, ultimately attaining an adult body condition that varies substantially between the sexes. For an adult female, the ultimate wet weight commonly reaches approximately 2,750 grams [Wwi = approximately 2,750 grams], although individual masses can fluctuate within a broader range depending on foraging success and reproductive state. Males, however, are typically heavier, with a mean asymptotic body mass of around 3,250 grams [Wwi = around 3,250 grams]. This sexual size dimorphism is a notable feature of the species and is likely linked to competitive dynamics at the breeding colony. The range of adult masses reported in the literature, spanning from as little as 1,900 grams to over 3,600 grams, underscores the considerable plasticity in body condition that these pelagic foragers exhibit in response to variable marine prey availability across their expansive North Pacific range.

At the elevated body temperature typical of an active procellariiform, approximately 39.4 °C [T = 39.4 °C], several key life-history milestones are reached in a predictable sequence. The fledgling chick achieves its first flight and departs the nest at 65 days after hatching [tx = 65 days after hatching], a developmental duration that is relatively abbreviated compared to many other large seabirds, reflecting the selective pressure to minimize the vulnerable nest-bound period on a predator-free oceanic island at a temperature of 39.4 °C [T = 39.4 °C]. Following this nutritional independence, the young immature bird embarks on an extended pelagic sojourn, during which it must hone its foraging skills. Gonadal maturation is a protracted process under these same thermal conditions, with puberty occurring at 195 days after hatching [tp = 195 days after hatching], signaling the onset of reproductive potential at a temperature of 39.4 °C [T = 39.4 °C].

Despite the attainment of physical maturity within the first year, Laysan albatrosses exhibit a markedly deferred reproductive schedule. Under the same thermal regime of 39.4 °C [T = 39.4 °C], the first successful brood is not typically produced until approximately 3,139 days since birth [tR = approximately 3,139 days since birth]. This protracted interval between puberty and first reproduction is characteristic of long-lived seabirds and is interpreted as an adaptive strategy that allows young birds to accumulate sufficient foraging experience and body condition to sustain the enormous energetic demands of incubating a single egg and rearing a chick. The species' maximum recorded longevity is equally impressive, with individuals documented to survive up to approximately 25,550 days [am = approximately 25,550 days], a lifespan that allows for many decades of reproductive contributions over a slow life-history trajectory, consistent with a low annual at a temperature of 39.4 °C [T = 39.4 °C]mortality rate.

Reproductive output in the Laysan albatross is constrained to a single egg per nesting attempt [N_R_i = single egg per nesting attempt], and successful pairs typically manage only one brood per year [F_R_i = one brood per year], reflecting the substantial biological investment required to provision a rapidly growing nestling over many weeks. This reproductive rate is exceptionally low in absolute terms but is offset by exceptional adult survival and a prolonged breeding lifespan. Females do not lay large clutches but instead channel all available energy into a single, large, yolk-rich egg. The maximum observed clutch frequency in the population is thus limited by the season length and the protracted incubation and chick-rearing phases, which together preclude a second successful breeding attempt within a single calendar year for any given pair at the core of their range.
